This section examines Q completed — Gemma
transfer from first

principles. Keep two questions separate:
does changing the order change

the measured outcome, and does the
proposed search method beat

a matched alternative at the same
distinct-evaluation budget? 4,101 calls;

120 orderings × 32 questions plus
retries/accounting; temperature zero.

Target order sensitivity: standard
deviation 0.247, range 0.06–0.91.

Fine-grained source-target rank
correlation: Spearman 0.158

weak and crossing zero. Position-effect
correlation: 0.064. Source top 15:

bottom five: 0.150 [0.088,0.200].
Interpretation at that point: bad extremes

transferred decisively; top performance
transferred weakly; fine-grained

structure did not. Now read evidence panel
Q-progress. The axes,

units, and sample are stated on screen.
The sample represented

here is 4,101 calls. Raw observations
remain visible wherever the

artifact provides them. Censored
observations stay marked at the cap

rather than becoming invented hitting
times, and sampled landscapes leave

unobserved permutations blank. The
supported finding is: Target order

sensitivity: standard deviation 0.247,
range 0.06–0.91. The broader claim

not established here is: The conclusion is
scoped to the

recorded evaluator, landscape, and budget.
This evidence changed the program

as follows: Carry this constraint into the
next experiment and

compare methods at equal cost. The
distinction is part of

the result. A large ordering effect does
not automatically imply

an evolutionary-search advantage, and
almost-sure convergence does not
promise practical efficiency.
